content: The required amount of energy derived from starchy staple foods is approximately 4%, leaving 19% of energy available for other foods and beverages. As the consumption of unhealthy items increases, the percentage of energy derived from dairy and protein foods decreases. When sweet biscuits are consumed daily for seven days a week, they displace nearly all other complementary foods and beverages. At nine months of age, an increase in servings of unhealthy items results in a reduction in the percentage of energy derived from starchy staples and fruits. When sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) or biscuits are included daily for seven days a week, the percentage of energy derived from vegetables and plant-based protein foods is reduced. Similarly, the inclusion of biscuits or crisps reduces the percentage of energy derived from fruits. When unhealthy items are consumed daily for seven days a week, starchy staples decrease, and protein foods increase. This may reflect the optimization of nutrient targets in the Optifood model, which minimizes protein foods once all nutrient requirements are met. Substituting unhealthy items with whole-grain foods could create new nutrient gaps, particularly for minerals, necessitating the selection of more nutrient-dense protein foods. For non-breastfed children, the results are similar to those of breastfed children of the same age. When three or seven servings of SSBs or biscuits are included, starchy staples decrease, and protein foods increase. However, instead of reducing fruits, added fats and oils are reduced when unhealthy items are consumed daily for seven days a week. Across all cases, macronutrient values remain within acceptable ranges, and there are no significant impacts from consuming one serving of any item per week or from including Super Cereal Plus at any frequency. When multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) and small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) are included three or seven days a week, there are differences of five percentage points or more in the percentage of energy derived from protein and fat, with varying changes in carbohydrate energy. Macronutrient values sometimes fall below or exceed recommended ranges, as shown in the results. For nine-month-old children, the percentage of energy from fat is influenced by the Optifood model, which minimizes protein once nutrient targets are met. The inclusion of MNPs and SQ-LNS often results in the selection of more added fats and oils, particularly for MNPs, which meet many micronutrient needs without contributing energy. When SQ-LNS or Super Cereal Plus is included daily for seven days a week, they displace most or all vegetables, dairy, and protein foods. When MNPs are included daily for seven days a week, nearly all protein foods are eliminated, but dairy consumption increases, likely due to the absence of calcium in MNPs. At lower frequencies (one or three days per week), animal-source protein foods decrease when MNPs or SQ-LNS are included, but not when Super Cereal Plus is included. The large reduction in protein foods with daily MNP inclusion reflects the meeting of iron targets, leading the Optifood model to minimize protein. For nine-month-old children, MNPs impact dietary patterns only when included daily for seven days a week. In this scenario, all target nutrient needs are met, but vegetables decrease, protein foods are nearly eliminated, and fruits, dairy, and added fats and oils increase. Including SQ-LNS daily for seven days a week reduces vegetables, eliminates fruits, and minimizes starchy staples, but does not substantially reduce protein foods, likely because iron needs are unmet. Super Cereal Plus has little impact when included one or three days a week but reduces the intake of all other food groups when included daily for seven days a week. In general, the inclusion of fortified items has the largest impact on dietary patterns for this age group. Fortified items decrease starchy staples and increase fruits in most scenarios. MNPs and SQ-LNS reduce animal-source protein foods and substantially increase added fats and oils. They also decrease vegetables when included daily for seven days a week. When included daily for seven days a week, Super Cereal Plus eliminates dairy and reduces all other food groups except plant-based protein foods. MNPs increase dairy consumption, while other fortified items decrease it. For nine-month-old children, the inclusion of fortified items increases the percentage of energy derived from fruits. MNPs and SQ-LNS reduce vegetables, but Super Cereal Plus does not. There are mixed impacts on dairy, with MNPs increasing it and both SQ-LNS and Super Cereal Plus decreasing it, particularly when included daily for seven days a week. There are small increases in protein foods in several scenarios, but the percentage of energy from protein foods remains low, reflecting the lack of gaps in target nutrients for this age group. The example food patterns provided are not recommendations but illustrations to assess the feasibility and validity of the model solutions. For instance, weekly patterns might include beef or sardines almost daily, small amounts of liver and tofu twice a week, and milk and cheese once a week. Quantities are approximate and based on total weekly grams divided by standard serving sizes. Nutrient content in these examples may differ from the modeled solutions, which use food subgroup nutrient profiles. In scenarios approximating real-world food patterns, diets in rural Bangladesh and Malawi are dominated by starchy staples, contributing 57%-68% of energy from complementary foods. In contrast, Mexican diets have more moderate amounts of starchy staples and higher proportions of dairy and other animal-source foods. Compared to best-case patterns, real-world diets in Bangladesh and Malawi have higher percentages of energy from starchy staples, added fats and oils, and unhealthy items, while energy from vegetables and animal-source protein foods is much lower. In Mexico, the percentage of energy from starchy staples is similar to best-case levels in infancy but lower for non-breastfed children. Best-case scenarios for non-breastfed children show very high percentages of energy from starchy staples, lower energy from vegetables, and higher energy from dairy. Protein energy is minimized in best-case scenarios, leading to lower percentages in infancy but higher percentages for non-breastfed children. Unhealthy items contribute significantly to energy intake for non-breastfed children in Mexico, accounting for 21% of total energy. Nutrient gaps are prevalent in real-world diets, particularly in Bangladesh and Malawi, where deficiencies in vitamins and minerals are more severe than in Mexico. Nutrient reference values (NRVs) are met for protein, α-linolenic acid, linoleic acid, vitamin A, vitamin C, and niacin equivalents across all age groups and settings. However, iron and vitamin D are consistently low, and B vitamins and minerals are well below NRVs in some or all age groups in Bangladesh and Malawi. Mexican scenarios also show deficiencies in several vitamins and minerals. The inclusion of fortified items such as MNPs, SQ-LNS, or Super Cereal Plus daily for seven days a week eliminates some nutrient gaps but leaves others. All three fortified items address gaps in B vitamins, but gaps for choline, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus remain in some age groups in Bangladesh and Malawi. Iron gaps are most effectively addressed by MNPs, followed by SQ-LNS, with Super Cereal Plus having a smaller impact. However, iron gaps persist in some scenarios, particularly with lower absorption assumptions. Upper limits (ULs) for zinc and copper are sometimes exceeded, especially with SQ-LNS and, to a lesser extent, MNPs.
